title: Beyond Qualcomm and Huawei's 6G Stack: The Missing Execution-Time Authority Plane
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction : Modern 6G, satellite, and AI-driven networks are becoming highly autonomous, fast, and difficult for humans to supervise in real time. Existing systems are very good at authentication, scheduling, orchestration, and communication efficiency, but they still leave an important gap: they do not reliably decide whether an action is actually permitted at the exact moment it becomes irreversible. In many cases, such as RF emission, packet forwarding, inter-satellite relay, or physical actuation, a wrong decision cannot be undone once execution begins. This paper introduces the Execution-Time Authority Plane (ETAP) to address that gap. ETAP places authority checking at the final point of execution and uses fail-closed, hardware-adjacent enforcement so that actions proceed only when valid real-time authority is present. Instead of relying mainly on post-event detection, audits, or software policy checks, the proposed approach aims to prevent unauthorized execution before irreversible effects occur. Foundational Concepts 1.1 Execution-Time Authority (Core Definition) Execution-Time Authority (ETA): Authority validation performed at execution finality—the moment when an action becomes physically or logically irreversible. Irreversibility Boundaries in 6G: RF Emission: Power amplifier enable, spectrum propagation Inter-Satellite Link (ISL) Forwarding: Fleet-wide propagation across optical mesh Persistent State Commits: Routing table updates, slice admission, settlement Physical Actuation: Thruster firing, antenna steering, attitude control AI Autonomous Actions: Decisions executing faster than human response (µs–ms) First-Principles Reality:Once RF energy leaves an antenna or fuel burns, physics prevents rollback. Therefore: Authority must be enforced at the same boundary and timescale as irreversibility. Anything earlier is advisory. Anything later is damage control. 1.2 Why This Is Not "Just Security" Traditional Security Execution-Time Authority Validates identity/credentials Validates execution permissibility Access control to resources Capability release at finality Policy enforcement via software Hardware-adjacent predicate evaluation Audit-based compliance Prevention-based compliance Operates on trust boundaries Operates on physics boundaries ETAP is execution semantics engineering, not an incremental security feature. 2. The 6G Patent Landscape: Where Industry Leaders Stop "100,000+ Standard-Essential Patents define how 6G communicates. Zero patents define whether 6G is permitted to execute." This section demonstrates why ETAP addresses a multi-billion dollar architectural void that Qualcomm, Huawei, and the entire 5G/6G patent ecosystem has not—and structurally cannot—solve with current approaches. 2.1 Understanding the SEP-Heavy Layers (Qualcomm & Huawei Dominance) Before defining what ETAP is, it's critical to understand what the 6G ecosystem already has—and more importantly, what structural gap remains despite 100,000+ declared Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs). The Patent Reality: Qualcomm: ~60,000+ declared 5G/6G SEPs (ETSI database) Huawei: ~50,000+ declared 5G/6G SEPs (ETSI database) Combined Coverage: ~40-50% of total 5G/6G SEP landscape These portfolios represent billions in R&D investment and define the fundamental mechanisms of modern wireless systems. Yet they leave a critical architectural gap that ETAP addresses. 2.2 Qualcomm's Domain: Device & Air-Interface Execution What Qualcomm Patents Comprehensively Cover: Technology Area Representative Coverage Example Patent Themes PHY Layer Channel coding (LDPC, Polar), modulation schemes, waveform generation How bits become radio signals MAC Scheduling HARQ procedures, resource allocation, scheduling algorithms How radio resources are shared Modem Architecture Baseband processing pipelines, DSP optimization, interference cancellation How signals are processed efficiently Mobility Handover procedures, beam management, cell selection/reselection How devices maintain connectivity Link Adaptation CQI reporting, MCS selection, power control How links optimize performance UE-Side Innovation Multi-antenna processing, CSI feedback, beam tracking How devices manage complex radios The Question Qualcomm Patents Answer: "How does a UE or RAN node implement radio procedures efficiently, correctly, and at scale?" What Qualcomm Patents Do NOT Answer: Whether RF emission is legally permitted in this jurisdiction right now Whether an AI-driven scheduling decision violates regulatory constraints at execution time How to prevent (not detect) spectrum violations before emission occurs How to block coerced commands that have valid cryptographic signatures How to enforce consumable quotas at hardware finality boundaries Example Gap Scenario: Qualcomm Patent: Efficient beam steering algorithm for mmWave 5G/6G Ensures: Beam points correctly, signal quality optimized Does NOT ensure: Beam direction complies with jurisdiction X at time T Emission quota not exceeded AI hasn't been poisoned to violate coverage rules → ETAP fills this gap by adding pre-emission authority gate 2.3 Huawei's Domain: Network Architecture & Orchestration What Huawei Patents Comprehensively Cover: Technology Area Representative Coverage Example Patent Themes Cloud-Native Core Service-Based Architecture (SBA), microservices, containerization How 5G core scales elastically Network Slicing Slice lifecycle management, resource isolation, SLA enforcement How multiple services coexist RAN Evolution C-RAN, Open RAN interfaces, RAN intelligence How RAN becomes programmable Automation Closed-loop control, intent-based networking, AI/ML orchestration How networks self-optimize Service Orchestration End-to-end service composition, multi-domain coordination How complex services are assembled Edge Computing MEC integration, compute offload, latency optimization How processing moves to edge The Question Huawei Patents Answer: "How should programmable, sliced, cloud-native 6G networks be architected, managed, and orchestrated?" abstract: Introduction : Modern 6G, satellite, and AI-driven networks are becoming highly autonomous, fast, and difficult for humans to supervise in real time. Existing systems are very good at authentication, scheduling, orchestration, and communication efficiency, but they still leave an important gap: they do not reliably decide whether an action is actually permitted at the exact moment it becomes irreversible. In many cases, such as RF emission, packet forwarding, inter-satellite relay, or physical actuation, a wrong decision cannot be undone once execution begins. This paper introduces the Execution-Time Authority Plane (ETAP) to address that gap. ETAP places authority checking at the final point of execution and uses fail-closed, hardware-adjacent enforcement so that actions proceed only when valid real-time authority is present. Instead of relying mainly on post-event detection, audits, or software policy checks, the proposed approach aims to prevent unauthorized execution before irreversible effects occur. Foundational Concepts 1.1 Execution-Time Authority (Core Definition) Execution-Time Authority (ETA): Authority validation performed at execution finality—the moment when an action becomes physically or logically irreversible. Irreversibility Boundaries in 6G: RF Emission: Power amplifier enable, spectrum propagation Inter-Satellite Link (ISL) Forwarding: Fleet-wide propagation across optical mesh Persistent State Commits: Routing table updates, slice admission, settlement Physical Actuation: Thruster firing, antenna steering, attitude control AI Autonomous Actions: Decisions executing faster than human response (µs–ms) First-Principles Reality:Once RF energy leaves an antenna or fuel burns, physics prevents rollback. Therefore: Authority must be enforced at the same boundary and timescale as irreversibility. Anything earlier is advisory. Anything later is damage control. 1.2 Why This Is Not "Just Security" Traditional Security Execution-Time Authority Validates identity/credentials Validates execution permissibility Access control to resources Capability release at finality Policy enforcement via software Hardware-adjacent predicate evaluation Audit-based compliance Prevention-based compliance Operates on trust boundaries Operates on physics boundaries ETAP is execution semantics engineering, not an incremental security feature. 2. The 6G Patent Landscape: Where Industry Leaders Stop "100,000+ Standard-Essential Patents define how 6G communicates. Zero patents define whether 6G is permitted to execute." This section demonstrates why ETAP addresses a multi-billion dollar architectural void that Qualcomm, Huawei, and the entire 5G/6G patent ecosystem has not—and structurally cannot—solve with current approaches. 2.1 Understanding the SEP-Heavy Layers (Qualcomm & Huawei Dominance) Before defining what ETAP is, it's critical to understand what the 6G ecosystem already has—and more importantly, what structural gap remains despite 100,000+ declared Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs). The Patent Reality: Qualcomm: ~60,000+ declared 5G/6G SEPs (ETSI database) Huawei: ~50,000+ declared 5G/6G SEPs (ETSI database) Combined Coverage: ~40-50% of total 5G/6G SEP landscape These portfolios represent billions in R&D investment and define the fundamental mechanisms of modern wireless systems. Yet they leave a critical architectural gap that ETAP addresses. 2.2 Qualcomm's Domain: Device & Air-Interface Execution What Qualcomm Patents Comprehensively Cover: Technology Area Representative Coverage Example Patent Themes PHY Layer Channel coding (LDPC, Polar), modulation schemes, waveform generation How bits become radio signals MAC Scheduling HARQ procedures, resource allocation, scheduling algorithms How radio resources are shared Modem Architecture Baseband processing pipelines, DSP optimization, interference cancellation How signals are processed efficiently Mobility Handover procedures, beam management, cell selection/reselection How devices maintain connectivity Link Adaptation CQI reporting, MCS selection, power control How links optimize performance UE-Side Innovation Multi-antenna processing, CSI feedback, beam tracking How devices manage complex radios The Question Qualcomm Patents Answer: "How does a UE or RAN node implement radio procedures efficiently, correctly, and at scale?" What Qualcomm Patents Do NOT Answer: Whether RF emission is legally permitted in this jurisdiction right now Whether an AI-driven scheduling decision violates regulatory constraints at execution time How to prevent (not detect) spectrum violations before emission occurs How to block coerced commands that have valid cryptographic signatures How to enforce consumable quotas at hardware finality boundaries Example Gap Scenario: Qualcomm Patent: Efficient beam steering algorithm for mmWave 5G/6G Ensures: Beam points correctly, signal quality optimized Does NOT ensure: Beam direction complies with jurisdiction X at time T Emission quota not exceeded AI hasn't been poisoned to violate coverage rules → ETAP fills this gap by adding pre-emission authority gate 2.3 Huawei's Domain: Network Architecture & Orchestration What Huawei Patents Comprehensively Cover: Technology Area Representative Coverage Example Patent Themes Cloud-Native Core Service-Based Architecture (SBA), microservices, containerization How 5G core scales elastically Network Slicing Slice lifecycle management, resource isolation, SLA enforcement How multiple services coexist RAN Evolution C-RAN, Open RAN interfaces, RAN intelligence How RAN becomes programmable Automation Closed-loop control, intent-based networking, AI/ML orchestration How networks self-optimize Service Orchestration End-to-end service composition, multi-domain coordination How complex services are assembled Edge Computing MEC integration, compute offload, latency optimization How processing moves to edge The Question Huawei Patents Answer: "How should programmable, sliced, cloud-native 6G networks be architected, managed, and orchestrated?" What Huawei Patents Do NOT Answer: How to physically prevent forwarding when jurisdiction constraints are violated How to enforce authority at µs timescales (orchestration operates at ms-second scales) How to create fail-closed execution gates that stop propagation under compromise How to implement hardware-adjacent veto mechanisms below orchestration layer How to prevent AI-driven cascade failures in NTN inter-satellite mesh Example Gap Scenario: Huawei Patent: Intelligent network slice orchestration with AI-driven resource allocation Ensures: Slices get resources efficiently, SLAs maintained Does NOT ensure: UPF cannot forward cross-border if jurisdiction token expired Satellite cannot emit if orbital position violates coverage bounds AI orchestrator decision physically blocked if authority absent → ETAP fills this gap by adding pre-forwarding/pre-emission finality gates 2.4 The Structural Gap: What 100,000+ SEPs Still Miss The Unasked Question in Current 6G Architecture: "Even if the system knows what to do and how to do it efficiently... is it permitted to execute right now?" This question becomes critical when: AI acts faster than governance (µs decision loops vs. human response times) Autonomous systems have no continuous oversight (NTN satellites, edge AI) Execution is physically irreversible (RF emission, ISL propagation, fuel burn) Coercion/compromise must be prevented, not just detected (zero-trust execution) Comparative Analysis: Architectural Question Qualcomm SEPs Huawei SEPs ETAP How to modulate/code signals? title: EESD special issue: AI and data‐driven methods in earthquake engineering – (Part 2)
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly important in earthquake engineering research, as it offers new possibilities for understanding, predicting, and mitigating the effects of earthquakes and related hazards. In the coming years, there will be continued research in AI-informed earthquake engineering that is focusing on ground motion modeling, geotechnical engineering, structural analysis, seismic design, health monitoring, multi-hazard assessment, and other areas, to enhance the safety and resilience of buildings and infrastructure. This is Part 2 of the special issue, whose topics include geotechnical engineering, structural analysis, design, health monitoring, damage evaluation, and seismic risk assessment. The first three articles in the Part 2 issue examine the application of AI and data-driven methods to geotechnical earthquake engineering. Hudson, Ulmer, Zimmaro, Kramer, Stewart, and Brandenberg propose an automated method for discretizing soil layers in cone penetration test (CPT) profiles using unsupervised machine learning (ML). The method aims to overcome the limitations of manual approaches that heavily rely on the analyst's experience and subjective judgment, which may lead to unrealistic results. Automated layer detection is achieved using a combination of agglomerative clustering and two cost functions to identify the optimal number of layers. The proposed algorithm is tested using 272 CPT profiles from the next generation liquefaction (NGL) database and is currently being used to develop liquefaction triggering and manifestation models. The results indicate that the proposed method has the potential to eliminate the bias induced by engineers. In spite of this, the authors recommend that the results from the automated detection be visually reviewed to ensure their validity. The paper by Hu, Xiong, Zhang, and Wang develops an approach to enhance the prediction accuracy of Bayesian network (BN) models used to evaluate earthquake-induced liquefaction settlement. The study deals with a specific limitation in existing BN models that require discretization of continuous variables, which limits predictions to categorical outcomes or ranges of settlement values. The authors address this challenge by proposing a hybrid approach that integrates domain knowledge with the hill-climbing algorithm in the formulation of a continuous BN regression model. The required conditional probability distributions of the parameters that define the BN model are computed based on historical liquefaction-induced settlement data and a Gaussian process learner. Using five-fold cross-validation, the authors show that the continuous BN model provides better generalization performance compared to previous approaches including those that employ the discrete BN classification strategy, simplified estimators such as the Tokimatsu–Seed and Ishihara–Yoshimine methods as well as an artificial neural network (ANN) model. Zhang, Ayello, Honegger, Bozorgnia, and Taciroglu develop an ML -based approach to predict the seismic response of fault-crossing natural gas pipelines, with the aim of improving the efficiency of time-consuming simulations. The study used the results from 217K nonlinear finite element analyses (FEA) for training and testing. Regression models based on ANNs are used as surrogate models for prediction. The input features cover various combinations of soil, structure, and fault attributes, and the output variable is the pipeline response under fault rupture displacement. The results from a case study indicated that the ANN method performs well, with the coefficient of determination R2 > 0.95. Based on the trained model and 14.5 million Monte Carlo-generated inputs, a large number of response predictions are obtained, forming a dataset that supplemented the missing input-output points in the 217K FEAs and improved the prediction accuracy. The following four articles aim to apply AI and data-driven methods to the advancement of structural seismic design and evaluation. Note that five more articles were published in Part 1 regarding the application to seismic design and analysis. Issa, Silva-Lopez, Baker, and Burton formulate an ML based optimization framework to support resilience-based design. More pointedly, an ML-driven surrogate model is used to capture the highly nonlinear relationship between the set of input variables used in the design and the building recovery performance. The surrogate model uses 43 design-related features as inputs and generates recovery time predictions, enabling (i) rapid estimation of recovery performance under a range of user-defined improvements, and (ii) implementation of complex and informative optimization techniques. The results from an application to a 3-story steel moment resisting frame office building showed that the surrogate model had a high prediction accuracy with the coefficient of determination R2 > 0.99, and reduced the computation time from 300 to 0.0002 s, further supporting the evaluation of the relationship between nonstructural and structural improvement strategies on recovery-based design. Liao, Wang, Fei, Huang, Xie, and Lu developed a physics-rule-co-guided self-supervised generative adversarial network (GAN) for determining the layout and mechanical properties of seismic isolation bearings. The self-supervised GAN addresses the limited availability of isolation design information that is needed to develop data-driven models. Four models comprise the intelligent design model including a physics estimator, rule evaluator, discriminator, and design generator. A deep neural network (DNN)-based surrogate model that predicts the response of the isolator is at the core of the physics estimator. A tensor operation-based loss calculator serves as the rule evaluator by ensuring that the design parameters are specified in accordance with the governing code or standard. The physics estimator and rule evaluator work together to guide the learning process of a GAN model without requiring ground truth data. A series of case studies were conducted using varying seismic intensities and building geometries. The results showed that the GAN design was consistent with the engineers’ design and was approximately 60 times more efficient than traditional engineering methods. A critical aspect of the design and performance assessment of base-isolated structures is ensuring that the axial pressure and shear deformation of the rubber bearings are within reasonable limits. Unlike pressure studies which consider the two loading mechanisms individually, the paper by Zeng, He, and Pan considers the coupling effect of axial pressure and shear deformation. Specifically, the authors develop a DNN to simultaneously detect the axial pressure and shear deformation in the rubber bearing of base isolators. Named pressure and deformation neural network (P&D-Net), the proposed model integrates wavelet packet decomposition with a fully connected neural network. The data set used to train the P&D-Net was derived from a series of full-scale physical tests performed on smart rubber bearings. By implementing a series of data-driven experiments, the study showed that the ability to accurately detect the axial pressure in the bearing is strongly influenced by the shear deformation and vice versa, thus highlighting the importance of considering the interaction between the two mechanisms. Furthermore, compared to a prior method which only used wave-let packets, the P&D-Net significantly improved the predictive performance. Guan and Burton formulate a computationally efficient method for performing collapse fragility assessment of building structures using the collaborative filtering (CF) technique. The CF-based collapse performance assessment procedure reduces the number of explicit simulations when conducting incremental dynamic analyses. The method randomly selects and runs a subset of the required nonlinear response history analyses (NRHAs) and uses CF to estimate the structural performance of the omitted cases. The results estimated by the CF are combined with that of the explicit NRHAs to obtain the corresponding fragility curves. The proposed method is applied to three archetype steel moment frame structures, and the results showed that the CF-based approach could reduce the required NTRAs by up to 50% while providing reliable collapse fragility estimates. Further, a series of sensitivity analyses showed that the method is robust to variations in key input parameters and the record-set used in the analyses. The following three articles apply AI and data-driven methods to advancing monitoring technologies for evaluating the behavior and performance of building structures. Note that four more articles on this sub-topic were published in Part 1. Eltouny and Liang present an uncertainty-aware early warning system that is specifically designed to avoid deep learning model mistakes and can provide near real-time structural health monitoring (SHM). The system utilizes a deep composite encoder-decoder network that combines elements from convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and variational inference to provide damage index distributions. The framework can detect anomalies in the structural system during seismic events and provide a measure of uncertainty that can be used to question the model's predictions. They apply their proposal to three real structures, two of which suffered damage during the 1994 Northridge earthquake. The framework is able to send a warning whenever damage is present. The results of the case study show that the number of warning signals sent correlates well with actual damage. In a comparative study, the proposed method is superior to two recently developed variational autoencoder (VAE)-based damage detection methods. Long-term SHM systems for large structures are known to suffer from data loss which reduces the reliability of near-real-time performance assessments. The paper by Zheng, Li, Li and Hao [Correction added on 2nd of August 2023, replaced author from Chou, Liu and Chang to Zheng, Li, Li and Hao.] implements a transformer-based GAN to reconstruct response measurements that are lost in SHM systems. Within the GAN, a multi-level wavelet-based discriminator is used to determine the degree of realism in the spectra of the reconstructed signals that are produced by the generator. The response reconstruction model was evaluated on two bridges at very different scales (pedestrian bridge and long-span vehicular traffic bridge), both equipped with SHM systems. The performance of the model was evaluated by establishing a relationship between the number of lost SHM channels and the response reconstruction error. For the pedestrian bridge, the error in the reconstructed response was limited to less than 25% even when five of the six channels were lost. When applied to the vehicular traffic bridge, the GAN limited the response reconstruction error to less than 30% despite losing half of the 16 channels that comprised the SHM system. Wang, Xu, Jing, Cui, Zhang, and Li formulated a deep learning model to automatically classify post-earthquake building damage from optical remote sensing images. Recognizing that several prior studies have developed image-based earthquake-induced building damage assessment models, the authors introduce a unique loss function that combines geometric consistency constraints (GCCs) with cross-entropy (CE). The GCC-CE-based loss function enhances the segmentation capability of the image classification model for buildings with complex geometries while providing superior overall performance at multiple scales. The GCC loss was designed to measure split line lengths, curvature, and area which facilitated more precise extraction of the complex geometries in damaged buildings. Compared to image-based damage detection models developed only using CE loss, the GCC-CE model reduced the duration of the training process which provided more accurate predictions. In terms of prediction accuracy, the GCC-CE-based loss model achieved the highest mean intersection over the union (mIoU) (86.98%). The specific improvements in segmentation capabilities include more reliable recognition of edge closures, removal of internal, and reduction of both false-positive and false-negative predictions. The last five articles apply AI and data-driven methods to seismic risk assessment at the regional scale and post-earthquake damage assessment of building structures. Kang, Kim, Kwon, and Song propose two frameworks for regional seismic loss assessment based on DNNs to extend the applicability of engineering demand parameter (EDP) residual estimation and improve its accuracy. The first framework estimates the EDP residuals of buildings by combining the EDP residuals of various single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) systems through modal combination rules. Three DNN models are constructed to predict the EDP residuals of SDOF systems. The second framework predicts the EDP residuals of buildings directly using the two DNN models. The accuracy of the two DNN-based frameworks is tested by comparing the results to those obtained from explicit response history analysis and the regression-based models. The numerical example demonstrated the importance of considering EDP residual correlation and the successful performance of the proposed frameworks in regional seismic loss assessment. Li, Farrar, and Yang develop a deep generative learning framework that achieves efficient regional seismic risk assessment. The method constructs input–output surrogate models of regional seismic risk by learning the underlying complex relation between earthquake source parameters and site-specific infrastructure performance at many locations from data. The learned deep surrogate models directly output the ground motion intensity map and the risk map of a region given the earthquake source parameters, circumventing the massive amounts of computation and data access that would be needed for site-specific assessments. They validate the presented framework on the bridge network risk assessment using simulated scenario earthquakes in the San Francisco Bay Area. They observe that the deep surrogate models perform well without the need for data access to locations and structures and are time-efficient (approximately 0.015 s). Galvis, Hulsey, Baker, and Deierlein presented a methodology to identify and evaluate relevant damage indicators that can be quantitatively related to safety thresholds using numerical simulations of damage. Ideally, these indicators should be insensitive to variability in the structural materials and model parameters. As such, the damage indicators are selected based on their reliability in estimating structural safety and the sensitivity to modeling uncertainty. The safety threshold for each damage indicator is selected to maximize accuracy in post-earthquake building assessments. The methodology is demonstrated through an application study of ductile reinforced concrete frame buildings. Results show that aggregated indices of structural component damage (e.g., aggregated over the floor of a building) have a level of accuracy of approximately 80% and outperform other damage indicators based on peak or residual drifts or simpler percentages of damaged components. It is noted that the methodology can be applied to a wider variety of structures to improve post-earthquake evaluation guidelines. Ahmed, Mangalathu, and Jeon proposed a stacked long short-term memory network to consider the influence of ground motion and structural characteristics on post-earthquake building damage assessment. Unlike previous studies, acceleration history and the number of stories are utilized to generalize the results for the same plan building frames with different numbers of stories. Three different approaches are presented in this work to link the ground motion history with the number of stories (2, 4, 8, 12, and 20 stories) in a reinforced concrete building frame, and the networks were tested using unseen ground motions. Of the three tested approaches, those providing good results were selected for further analysis. For the approaches chosen, the network architectures were changed to a diamond shape and an autoencoder-like shape with more hidden units (to obtain higher accuracy), which were tested on frames with unseen plan layouts. The adopted approaches produced high predictive accuracy (80%−90%) and low training time. The proposed model shows superior performance relative to previously developed techniques. Bhatta and Dang perform ML-based seismic damage prediction of RC buildings, while considering both seismic and structural parameters. The paper first evaluates the feasibility of using ML techniques such as K-nearest neighbor, random forest, decision tree, support vector machine, and ANN to rapidly predict earthquake-induced reinforced concrete building damage considering both the structural properties and ground motion characteristics. Then, the ML models are trained using the simulation results. Due to a lack of real earthquake damage datasets, most prior related studies utilized simulation data to develop ML-based earthquake damage prediction models. In contrast, this study uses real earthquake damage data for RC buildings collected after the 2015 Nepal Earthquake. An overall accuracy of more than 62% is obtained for the test set. The study demonstrates that ML algorithms are capable of rapidly predicting the seismic damage of reinforced concrete buildings with reasonable accuracy. Based on the 28 articles published in Part 1 and Part 2 of the special issue and a review of the broader literature, we present the following brief outlook on how AI can be further integrated into earthquake engineering research and practice: It is expected that there will be an increased focus on developing hybrid models that combine physics-based simulations with AI-based approaches to improve the accuracy of ground motion prediction models while reducing computational costs. AI-based methods will also continue to improve our understanding of geotechnical earthquake engineering such as soil-structure interaction and liquefaction potential. AI-infused structural analysis and performance assessment models will be trained on increasingly larger and more generalizable datasets and used to predict structural response, damage, and collapse, and develop optimal retrofit schemes and smart materials. AI has the potential to revolutionize SHM by providing real-time assessment of buildings and infrastructure during and after earthquakes. Additionally, AI-based methods will be implemented to evaluate the combined effects of earthquakes and other hazards, such as tsunamis, landslides, and floods, by modeling their complex interactions and impacts on the built environment. It is noteworthy that Generative AI, or AI Generated Content (AIGC), offers numerous opportunities to revolutionize many fields, including earthquake engineering. For example, AIGC can automate the generation of structural layout designs that use appropriate materials and maintain desired performance levels under earthquake loading. Additionally, AIGC can facilitate rapid digital prototyping by automatically populating design spaces and identifying the solution(s) that minimizes cost and environmental impacts while achieving the desired performance objectives. The integration of AI into earthquake engineering is poised to transform the field, enabling more accurate predictions, innovative designs, and enhanced infrastructure resilience to seismic hazards. However, as AI techniques continue to develop, researchers and practitioners must collaborate closely to ensure the successful implementation of these methods. It is through this collaboration that the full potential of AI will be leveraged to mitigate the risks associated with earthquakes and related hazards. The guest editors would like to thank Masayoshi Nakashima, the Executive Editor, for his leadership of the journal and the support and guidance provided for this Special Issue. Additionally, the overwhelming response of the earthquake engineering research community to the call for papers as part of this special issue is acknowledged. Finally, this issue, as well as all refereed journals, would not be possible without the diligent reviews provided by peers within the earthquake engineering community. As such, the guest editors wish to thank the individuals that participated in the review process.

title: Introduction to the Special Issue on Evolving IoT and Cyber-Physical Systems: Advancements, Applications, and Solutions
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) is regarded as a next-generation wave of Information Technology (IT) after the widespread emergence of the Internet and mobile communication technologies. IoT supports information exchange and networked interaction of appliances, vehicles and other objects, making sensing and actuation possible in a low-cost and smart manner. On the other hand, cyber-physical systems (CPS) are described as the engineered systems which are built upon the tight integration of the cyber entities (e.g., computation, communication, and control) and the physical things (natural and man-made systems governed by the laws of physics). The IoT and CPS are not isolated technologies. Rather it can be said that IoT is the base or enabling technology for CPS and CPS is considered as the grownup development of IoT, completing the IoT notion and vision. Both are merged into closed-loop, providing mechanisms for conceptualizing, and realizing all aspects of the networked composed systems that are monitored and controlled by computing algorithms and are tightly coupled among users and the Internet. That is, the hardware and the software entities are intertwined, and they typically function on different time and location-based scales. In fact, the linking between the cyber and the physical world is enabled by IoT (through sensors and actuators). CPS that includes traditional embedded and control systems are supposed to be transformed by the evolving and innovative methodologies and engineering of IoT. Several applications areas of IoT and CPS are smart building, smart transport, automated vehicles, smart cities, smart grid, smart manufacturing, smart agriculture, smart healthcare, smart supply chain and logistics, etc. Though CPS and IoT have significant overlaps, they differ in terms of engineering aspects. Engineering IoT systems revolves around the uniquely identifiable and internet-connected devices and embedded systems; whereas engineering CPS requires a strong emphasis on the relationship between computation aspects (complex software) and the physical entities (hardware). Engineering CPS is challenging because there is no defined and fixed boundary and relationship between the cyber and physical worlds. In CPS, diverse constituent parts are composed and collaborated together to create unified systems with global behaviour. These systems need to be ensured in terms of dependability, safety, security, efficiency, and adherence to real‐time constraints. Hence, designing CPS requires knowledge of multidisciplinary areas such as sensing technologies, distributed systems, pervasive and ubiquitous computing, real-time computing, computer networking, control theory, signal processing, embedded systems, etc. CPS, along with the continuous evolving IoT, has posed several challenges. For example, the enormous amount of data collected from the physical things makes it difficult for Big Data management and analytics that includes data normalization, data aggregation, data mining, pattern extraction and information visualization. Similarly, the future IoT and CPS need standardized abstraction and architecture that will allow modular designing and engineering of IoT and CPS in global and synergetic applications. Another challenging concern of IoT and CPS is the security and reliability of the components and systems. Although IoT and CPS have attracted the attention of the research communities and several ideas and solutions are proposed, there are still huge possibilities for innovative propositions to make IoT and CPS vision successful. The major challenges and research scopes include system design and implementation, computing and communication, system architecture and integration, application-based implementations, fault tolerance, designing efficient algorithms and protocols, availability and reliability, security and privacy, energy-efficiency and sustainability, etc. It is our great privilege to present Volume 21, Issue 3 of Scalable Computing: Practice and Experience. We had received 30 research papers and out of which 14 papers are selected for publication. The objective of this special issue is to explore and report recent advances and disseminate state-of-the-art research related to IoT, CPS and the enabling and associated technologies. The special issue will present new dimensions of research to researchers and industry professionals with regard to IoT and CPS. Vivek Kumar Prasad and Madhuri D Bhavsar in the paper titled "Monitoring and Prediction of SLA for IoT based Cloud described the mechanisms for monitoring by using the concept of reinforcement learning and prediction of the cloud resources, which forms the critical parts of cloud expertise in support of controlling and evolution of the IT resources and has been implemented using LSTM. The proper utilization of the resources will generate revenues to the provider and also increases the trust factor of the provider of cloud services. For experimental analysis, four parameters have been used i.e. CPU utilization, disk read/write throughput and memory utilization. Kasture et al. in the paper titled "Comparative Study of Speaker Recognition Techniques in IoT Devices for Text Independent Negative Recognition" compared the performance of features which are used in state of art speaker recognition models and analyse variants of Mel frequency cepstrum coefficients (MFCC) predominantly used in feature extraction which can be further incorporated and used in various smart devices. Mahesh Kumar Singh and Om Prakash Rishi in the paper titled "Event Driven Recommendation System for E-Commerce using Knowledge based Collaborative Filtering Technique" proposed a novel system that uses a knowledge base generated from knowledge graph to identify the domain knowledge of users, items, and relationships among these, knowledge graph is a labelled multidimensional directed graph that represents the relationship among the users and the items. The proposed approach uses about 100 percent of users' participation in the form of activities during navigation of the web site. Thus, the system expects under the users' interest that is beneficial for both seller and buyer. The proposed system is compared with baseline methods in area of recommendation system using three parameters: precision, recall and NDGA through online and offline evaluation studies with user data and it is observed that proposed system is better as compared to other baseline systems. Benbrahim et al. in the paper titled "Deep Convolutional Neural Network with TensorFlow and Keras to Classify Skin Cancer" proposed a novel classification model to classify skin tumours in images using Deep Learning methodology and the proposed system was tested on HAM10000 dataset comprising of 10,015 dermatoscopic images and the results observed that the proposed system is accurate in order of 94.06\% in validation set and 93.93\% in the test set. Devi B et al. in the paper titled "Deadlock Free Resource Management Technique for IoT-Based Post Disaster Recovery Systems" proposed a new class of techniques that do not perform stringent testing before allocating the resources but still ensure that the system is deadlock-free and the overhead is also minimal. The proposed technique suggests reserving a portion of the resources to ensure no deadlock would occur. The correctness of the technique is proved in the form of theorems. The average turnaround time is approximately 18\% lower for the proposed technique over Banker's algorithm and also an optimal overhead of O(m). Deep et al. in the paper titled "Access Management of User and Cyber-Physical Device in DBAAS According to Indian IT Laws Using Blockchain" proposed a novel blockchain solution to track the activities of employees managing cloud. Employee authentication and authorization are managed through the blockchain server. User authentication related data is stored in blockchain. The proposed work assists cloud companies to have better control over their employee's activities, thus help in preventing insider attack on User and Cyber-Physical Devices. Sumit Kumar and Jaspreet Singh in paper titled "Internet of Vehicles (IoV) over VANETS: Smart and Secure Communication using IoT" highlighted a detailed description of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) with current applications, architectures, communication technologies, routing protocols and different issues. The researchers also elaborated research challenges and trade-off between security and privacy in area of IoV. Deore et al. in the paper titled "A New Approach for Navigation and Traffic Signs Indication Using Map Integrated Augmented Reality for Self-Driving Cars" proposed a new approach to supplement the technology used in self-driving cards for perception. The proposed approach uses Augmented Reality to create and augment artificial objects of navigational signs and traffic signals based on vehicles location to reality. This approach help navigate the vehicle even if the road infrastructure does not have very good sign indications and marking. The approach was tested locally by creating a local navigational system and a smartphone based augmented reality app. The approach performed better than the conventional method as the objects were clearer in the frame which made it each for the object detection to detect them. Gopal Ayengar Memorial Oration Lecture Logic and Necessities in the Repair of IR-induced DSBs: Defining Parameters George Iliakis Department of Radiation Therapy, Division of Experimental Radiation Biology, University Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen, Essen, Germany E-mail: [email protected] Double strand breaks (DSBs) are induced in the DNA after exposure of cells to ionizing radiation (IR) and are highly dangerous for genome integrity. Erroneous processing of DSBs is a cause of cell death, or its transformation to a cancer cell. Four mechanistically distinct pathways have evolved in cells of higher eukaryotes to process DSBs, providing thus multiple options for the damaged cells. HR removes DSBs in an error-free manner. c-NHEJ removes DSBs with high speed, but can introduce errors and cause chromosomal translocations. alt-EJ operates on similar principles as c-NHEJ but is slower and more error-prone. Finally, SSA is active in repeat-regions of the genome and is associated with deletion of the DNA flanking the regions of homology. It is evident that the four repair pathways available for the processing of DSBs are not alternative options having equivalent outcomes for the genome and that all but HR are error-prone. We use immunofluorescence; high-throughput image analysis; western blotting and other standard biological techniques. Cells are irradiated with X-rays and well as with high LET particles. I will discuss the rationale for the evolution of pathways with such divergent properties and fidelities and outline the logic and necessities that govern their engagement and parameters that determine it. I will reason that for the most part, cells are not free to choose one specific pathway for the processing of a DSB, but rather they engage one by logic, striving for the highest fidelity selection, adapted to necessities imposed by the character of the DSB and the cell cycle phase in which it is induced. I will present evidence for uncharacterized processes that prevent the stochastic engagement of a particular pathway, owing only to the coincidental presence of related activities in the vicinity of the DSB. I will speculate how this form of DSB repair pathway wiring explains radiosensitization by different compounds, including inhibitors of DSB repair enzymes. In addition, I will introduce DSB clusters as a particularly consequential form of chromatin breakage and review findings suggesting that this form of damage underpins the increased efficacy of high LET radiation modalities. These concepts have implications for the protection of humans from terrestrial and space radiation and present opportunities for the improvement of cancer treatment with radiations, including of high LET radiations. Singh Memorial Oration Lecture Radiation and Chromosome Satoshi Tashiro Department of Cellular Biology, Research Institute for Radiation Biology and Medicine, Hiroshima University, Hiroshima, Japan E-mail: [email protected] Human chromosomal DNA, which encodes our genetic information, is constantly subjected to damage from natural radiation sources, ultraviolet rays, and other environmental factors. The integrity of this DNA is preserved through intricate DNA repair mechanisms that are tailored to the type and severity of the damage. However, errors in these repair processes can lead to chromosomal aberrations, genetic mutations, and other alterations in genetic information, ultimately contributing to diseases such as leukemia and cancer, which are known to result from radiation exposure. In this context, the DNA repair system and the higher-order nuclear architecture are crucial in managing chromosome aberrations, particularly structural abnormalities. Several proteins, including γH2AX, MRE11, 53BP1, and RAD51, are integral to the formation of radiation-induced nuclear foci (RINF), which play a vital role in DNA repair. Our research has particularly focused on RAD51, a key protein in the recombinational repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Through the development of a UVA micro irradiation system, we first demonstrated that RAD51 forms nuclear foci at DNA damage sites. Further investigations using advanced bio-imaging techniques revealed that RAD51 focus formation is regulated by complex systems, including histone modifications, nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling, and SUMO modifications. Notably, we found that excessive accumulation of RAD51 at damage sites could lead to chromosomal aberrations. Leveraging our expertise in DNA repair, we developed the PNA-FISH technique for high-throughput chromosome analysis in biological dosimetry. This technique enables the detection of chromosomal abnormalities induced by low dose irradiation from CT scans. Furthermore, we established that chromosomal aberrations could serve as biomarkers for predicting the side effects of radiation therapy. High-throughput chromosome analysis via PNA-FISH holds significant potential as a biological dosimetry tool in radiation emergency medicine and as a biomarker of radiation sensitivity in radiology and radiation oncology. The International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005 are a legally binding agreement of 196 countries to develop the capability to detect and report public health emergencies worldwide. IHR require that all countries have the ability to detect, assess, report, and respond to public health events. This international law was enacted on 15 June 2007 to prevent, protect against, control and provide a public health response to the international spread of disease in ways that are commensurate with and restricted to public health risks, and which avoid unnecessary interference with international traffic and trade. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) works with countries to comply with the IHR (2005). The CDC’s global programs address health threats and conditions that are major causes of death, disease, and disability. Radiological and nuclear threats have driven renewed research interest in developing medical countermeasures for clinically significant ionizing radiation exposure.
